p1_yt1: Same operator, different pieces: build one sentence out of three separate `const` strings, with the spaces in the right places. Then print `typeof ("id" + 42)` and confirm for yourself that the result is a string, not a number.
p1_yt2: Same generator, a shorter slice: keep 4 characters instead of 6, and print the length to prove you got 4. Run the cell three or four times and watch the value change each time — that unpredictability is the whole feature.
p1_yt3: Same technique, a different template: build a unique username and embed it in a CSS selector string (`"input[name='" + unique + "']"`) instead of an XPath one. Print both the value and the finished selector — string-building does not care which locator syntax it is feeding.
p2_yt1: Same idea, a different field: generate a unique phone number — digits only, no `@example.com` on the end — and fill it into the `input[type='tel']` field. Getting this right now makes Problem 3 mostly typing.
p2_yt2: Same proof, a different field: fill First Name with a generated value, then count `//input[@value='...']` for that value and print `.inputValue()` next to it. Confirm the count is 0 here too — so you know it is a rule about every plain `<input>`, not something peculiar to the email box.
p2_yt3: Same pattern, a different control: let `Math.random()` choose between the two checkbox ids you know (`#checkbox1` and `#checkbox2`), build the selector by concatenating the number onto `"#checkbox"`, then check it and print which one it picked.
p2_yt4: Same two functions, the opposite direction: write the `text()` XPath that *does* match the heading, by putting the real trailing space inside your string. Then confirm `normalize-space()` still matches it as well. Both find it — and you will not want to maintain the first one.
